blocks.text: Paul opens by defining apostles as 'ministers of Christ' and 'stewards of the mysteries of God.' The steward image emphasizes delegated responsibility: an apostle holds office not by personal right but by appointment, and faithfulness to the trust, not public acclaim, is what matters. Verse 2 makes the standard explicit: 'It is required in stewards that one be found faithful.'

Paul then dismisses premature judgment of his conduct. He does not defend himself against Corinthian verdicts but states he does not even judge himself. Yet this is not moral complacency: his lack of self-condemnation does not vindicate him. Hidden motives and true fidelity belong to God's final examination. The Lord alone will 'bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the purposes of the hearts' (4:5), postponing any definitive verdict until that day.

Paul introduces an opaque formula: 'do not go beyond what is written' and applies it to himself and Apollos as a cautionary case study. The phrase is spare and its full meaning uncertain, but its immediate effect is clear: it checks the Corinthians' tendency to elevate one teacher against another. The goal is humility, preventing factional pride from cleaving the church.

sections.title: The Irony of Achievement and Pride (4:7-8)

blocks.text: Paul hammers at Corinthian self-regard with three crushing questions: 'Who distinguishes you? What do you have that you did not receive? If you received it, why boast as if you did not receive it?' Every human distinction—whether learning, Spirit-gifting, or virtue—is received, not earned. To boast of it is absurd and ungrateful. Verse 8 sharpens the irony: the Corinthians speak and act as though they are already filled, already rich, already reigning. Paul's tone is biting because their confidence ignores both the present order and apostolic reality.

The passage pivots to a searing catalog of apostolic deprivation. Paul and his colleagues are 'fools for Christ's sake' while Corinthians glory in wisdom; they are weak while Corinthians are strong. Verses 11-13 expand: apostles hunger, thirst, go naked, are beaten, have no fixed home, toil with their own hands, endure reviling, persecution, and defamation. They are 'made as the filth of the world, the offscouring of all things.' The stark contrast—Corinthian fullness against apostolic spectacle—exposes the gap between imagined apostolic comfort and actual apostolic condition.

sections.title: Admonition Rooted in Love and Fatherhood (4:14-15)

blocks.text: Paul shifts tone sharply: 'I do not write these things to shame you, but to admonish you as my beloved children.' The correction is real, but the relationship is one of familial love. He claims spiritual fatherhood: 'Though you have ten thousand instructors in Christ, you do not have many fathers; for I became your father through the gospel.' Fatherhood here is not control or possession but a bond of origin and responsibility. His admonition, however pointed, flows from that kinship.
